summary: A proposal to remove the 30-second delay the IMP imposes before accepting input from a Host that has just come up. The delay lets the news that the Host is up spread through the network. It explains why the delay existed and how the aim could be met in another way.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 410 proposes removing a 30-second wait after a host starts. Instead, the destination IMP would decide whether its own host was ready when a message arrived.

subtitle: A proposal to remove the IMP's host startup delay

tldr.problem: An IMP waited 30 seconds after a host came up so other IMPs could learn that the host was available.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal moves dead-host detection from the sending IMP to the destination IMP, which directly knows whether its attached host is ready.
tldr.outcome: A host could send as soon as it raised its ready line, while dead-destination errors might take longer to return and could arrive out of order.

today: RFC 410 proposes a change to how IMPs handle hosts that have just come up. The RFC says the change would take effect at a scheduled software release if sites raised no adverse comments.

sections.title: Why Hosts Had to Wait
sections.content: An IMP currently waited 30 seconds before accepting input from a host that had just come up. The delay allowed information about that host's status to propagate through the network. Without it, another host might send a message before the destination IMP knew the destination was up, and the reply could be discarded as addressed to a dead host.
sections.plainLanguage: The wait gave other IMPs time to learn that a host had started. Without that information, a message or reply could be treated as going to a dead destination.

sections.title: Detecting Dead Hosts at the Destination
sections.content:
The proposal removes the 30-second delay and has the destination IMP check whether its own host is ready. When the host raises its ready line, the IMP can accept input immediately. When a message arrives for a host that is not ready, the destination IMP can return a destination-dead message.

This avoids making every host wait for the worst-case time for routing information to spread.
sections.plainLanguage: The host's own IMP can check whether it is ready. This would let the host send without waiting for distant IMPs to update their information.

sections.title: Effects on Hosts and Error Messages
sections.content:
The RFC says host software would not need to change. Hosts could send as soon as their ready line came up or wait as before. They might remove startup delays in their own routines because those would no longer be necessary.

Destination-dead messages would take longer to reach the source because they travel through the network, and multiple such messages might return out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts would not need new software to use the change. Error messages might take longer to return and might not arrive in the same order as the original messages.
